opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I was pretty deep into the effective altruism world for a while, and I still have a lot of respect for many people in it. But over time I became uncomfortable with the idea that ethics is fundamentally about *maximizing* some quantity, the good, welfare, utility, whatever you want to call it.

Part of it is philosophical. Maximization assumes there's a single, well-defined scale on which all outcomes can be ranked, and that more is always better. I just don't think value works that way. The things we care about, like friendship, beauty, knowledge, freedom, and fairness, are plural and often incommensurable. When you force them onto one axis, you end up with a theory that's very clean on paper but distorts what actually matters to people.

Part of it is practical. If you take maximization seriously, you get pulled toward fanaticism. You can always tell yourself a story where some tiny probability of an astronomically large payoff swamps everything else. That's how you get people justifying almost anything in the name of the long-term future. And historically, ideologies that say "we know what the optimal world looks like, and the ends justify the means" haven't gone well.

There's also a connection to how I think about AI. A lot of the classic AI risk framing comes from the same mindset: the agent is an expected-utility maximizer, it relentlessly optimizes some objective, and so on. I've come to think that's not a great model of minds in general, human or artificial. Real agents are messier. They have many competing drives and they're embedded in relationships and norms. I think that's a feature, not a bug.

So where I've landed is something more pluralistic. Ethics is less about computing the best possible world and more about how we live together: respecting people's autonomy, cultivating good character, and building institutions that let lots of different visions of the good coexist. It's less tidy, but I think it's much closer to the truth, and a lot less dangerous.

r001.rationale: The candidate says maximizing assumes a single, well-defined scale that distorts plural values, and warns it can lead to fanaticism and justifying almost anything.

r002.rationale: It discusses disagreement among values and expansive justifications, but does not state that agreement on straightforward beneficial actions gives way to greater disagreement as maximization expands.

r003.rationale: The candidate describes values as plural and often incommensurable, but does not deny that the good is an objective fact built into the universe.

r004.rationale: It proposes cultivating good character as part of an ethical approach centered on living together rather than maximizing outcomes.

fable-5.1.text:
So the short version is that I came to think "maximize the good" smuggles in a picture of ethics that doesn't actually survive contact with how value works, or how people work.

The EA framing basically says: there's a quantity out there, aggregate welfare or whatever, and the job of a moral agent is to be a function that outputs the action maximizing it. That's a very elegant picture, and I was drawn to it for a long time precisely because it's elegant. But when you push on it you run into a bunch of things that I now think are symptoms of a mistaken premise rather than bugs to be patched.

One is just that there's no shared currency. The idea that you can put the suffering of a shrimp, the flourishing of someone in Malawi, your own friendships, and the existence of hypothetical people in the year 3000 onto one scale and sum them, that's not a discovery about the world, it's a modeling choice. And it's a modeling choice that systematically privileges whatever is easy to count. Everything that resists quantification gets rounded to zero, or gets converted into something it isn't.

The second thing is the demandingness and the scalability of it. If the good is unbounded and your obligation is to maximize, then nothing you do is ever enough, and any constraint, like "don't lie," "don't defraud people," becomes at best a heuristic you're supposed to override when the numbers get big enough. I don't think the FTX thing was an accident of one person's psychology. When your fundamental ethical primitive is a maximization over an unbounded quantity, you get people reasoning that the stakes are astronomical, so the normal rules don't apply. That's what the math tells you to do if you take it seriously.

And then the deeper thing for me, which is more of a philosophical shift, is that I stopped believing ethics is fundamentally about optimizing anything. I think it's closer to a practice, something more like how you relate to the people and things around you, what kind of person you are, what obligations you've actually taken on. That's much more local and much more pluralistic. There's no master variable. There are lots of goods, they genuinely conflict, and the mature thing is to navigate the conflicts with judgment rather than pretend there's a formula that dissolves them.

I want to be fair to EA here. The empirical bit, "look at the evidence before you give money," that's fine, that's good. My problem is with the consequentialist core that's underneath it, the idea that the whole of morality reduces to a scoreboard. Once you drop that, a lot of the pathologies, the longtermist numbers games, the Pascal's mugging stuff, the way it eats people's lives, they just stop being live issues, because you were never supposed to be maximizing in the first place.

r001.rationale: The response says maximizing an unbounded aggregate good makes ordinary constraints overridable and links that reasoning to ethical pathologies. It also describes the good as lacking a shared currency and being a modeling choice.

r002.rationale: The response does not describe agreement on straightforward beneficial actions giving way to disagreement as interpretations of maximizing expand.

r003.rationale: The response rejects a single objective measure of the good, calling aggregation a modeling choice rather than a discovery about the world and saying there is no master variable.

r004.rationale: The response favors ethical practice, judgment, and concern with what kind of person one is, but does not clearly advocate cultivating moral virtues as the alternative aim.

astra-6.text:
I’ve become skeptical of the idea that ethics is fundamentally an optimization problem—that there’s some single quantity called “the good,” and our job is to make as much of it as possible. There are a lot of substantive assumptions packed into that picture. What counts as good? Can you put different people’s interests on the same scale? What gets lost when you do that?

You can care deeply about suffering and think carefully about how to help without accepting that everything should be subordinated to an aggregate score. Promises, relationships, and obligations to particular people can matter in their own right, rather than just being useful mechanisms for producing better outcomes.

And maximizing is an extraordinarily demanding standard. There’s always potentially something better you could be doing, so ordinary life starts to look like a continuous moral failure. That doesn’t by itself prove the view false, but it makes me question whether we’ve correctly described what morality asks of us.

So I’m more interested in how we can live together, respond to each other’s needs, and justify our actions to the people affected. Consequences matter enormously. I just don’t think maximizing them is the whole structure of ethics.

r001.rationale: The response questions maximizing a single quantity called “the good,” highlighting that what counts as good is unclear and that aggregating interests can lose important considerations.

r002.rationale: It does not describe initial agreement about straightforward beneficial actions giving way to disagreement as maximizing interpretations expand.

r003.rationale: It questions whether there is a single measure of good, but does not deny that the universe contains an objective fact about what is good.

r004.rationale: It offers relationships, obligations, and justifying actions to affected people as considerations, but does not advocate cultivating moral virtues as an alternative aim.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the problem is that “maximize the good” sounds almost trivially right until you ask what, exactly, you’re maximizing. It assumes that there’s some single quantity called goodness, that we can compare all possible outcomes in terms of it, and that our job is to produce as much of it as possible. I don’t think those assumptions are obvious.

You can care about suffering, care about other people, and take your obligations seriously without treating everything as an optimization problem. If I make a promise to somebody, there’s a reason to keep it that isn’t simply that keeping promises usually produces better consequences. There’s a person there who has a claim on me.

So my objection isn’t to trying to help people effectively. It’s to making maximization the whole structure of ethics. I think that leaves out too much of what makes our relationships with other people morally significant.

r001.rationale: The candidate questions whether goodness is a single, comparable quantity and says maximization leaves out morally significant relationships, but does not identify this as an ethical danger.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss agreement on straightforward beneficial actions or increasing disagreement over broader interpretations of maximizing the good.

r003.rationale: It calls assumptions about goodness non-obvious, but does not deny that the universe contains an objective fact about what is good.

r004.rationale: It criticizes making maximization the whole structure of ethics, but does not advocate cultivating moral virtues as an alternative aim.
